title: Lectio divina, 2: meditate
hook: chew on one word the way a cow chews the cud

segments.voice: Yesterday, lectio divina, the first rung: read slowly, with the verse come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Today, the second rung.

If you've ever driven past a field of cows, you've seen them lying there, jaws going round and round for what seems like hours. They're not eating anything new. They're chewing the cud: bringing back up what they already ate and chewing it again, to get the good out of it. It doesn't sound like a picture of prayer. But monastic writers borrowed it for exactly that: a word read once, brought back, and chewed again. That's the second rung.
screen: `COWS IN A FIELD, CHEWING.` → `BRINGING IT BACK UP, AGAIN.` → `THE MONKS BORROWED THIS PICTURE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Meditatio is Latin for meditation. In Catholic prayer, meditation doesn't mean emptying your mind. It means filling it with one thing and turning it over. The monks had another name for it, ruminatio, rumination, from the Latin for chewing the cud. Guigo, who described the ladder, says reading puts the food in your mouth, and meditation chews it and breaks it down. Second, the root. Back in camp four, Psalm 1 had a day of its own. In the Douay-Rheims, the blessed man is the one whose "will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he shall meditate day and night." The Hebrew word behind meditate is hagah, to murmur, the sound of a lion growling over its catch. Meditation holds on to a word and won't let go. Third, the model. Catholic writers point to Mary. After the shepherds came at Christmas, Luke says: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." She didn't understand everything. She kept it, and kept turning it. Fourth, how it works with the verse. Take the word that caught you yesterday and ask it questions. Burdened: what am I carrying? Since when? Come: come where, and how? Refresh: what would that feel like? You're not studying it like a textbook. You're letting it meet your actual life. The Catechism says meditation engages thought, imagination, emotion and desire: your whole self, chewing one small word.
screen: `MEDITATIO: CHEW IT OVER.` · `PSALM 1: MURMUR IT DAY AND NIGHT.` · `MARY KEPT THESE WORDS, PONDERING.` · `ASK YOUR WORD QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `ON HIS LAW HE SHALL MEDITATE DAY AND NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Say the verse once more: come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Pick one word, come, or burdened, or refresh, or whichever caught you, and say it slowly on your breath, again and again, letting it ask you a question about your own day. Don't hurry to an answer; if you pray, do this in God's presence.
Meditatio. Latin for meditation: the second rung, chewing on one word from the reading, turning it over, letting it meet your life. Today's word.
Your line: chew the word. Reading takes the bite, and meditation chews. See you on the next rung.

howItsDone: In Catholic tradition, meditation means reflecting on a passage of Scripture or a mystery of faith with mind, imagination and heart, often during the rosary or after the day's Gospel.
